faqs.question: What is an OCT scan of the eye?
faqs.answer: OCT (Optical Coherence Tomography) is a non-invasive imaging test that uses light waves to take detailed cross-sectional pictures of your retina — the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. It can measure retinal thickness and detect abnormalities at the micron level. It's like an 'MRI of the eye' but faster and completely painless.

faqs.question: Is OCT scan painful?
faqs.answer: Not at all. OCT is completely non-invasive and painless. You simply look at a target light while the machine scans your eye — there is no contact with the eye, no dye injection, and no radiation. The scan takes only a few seconds per eye.

whatIsIt: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a revolutionary, non-invasive imaging test that uses light waves to take microscopic, cross-sectional pictures of your retina. It is akin to an 'ultrasound using light.' This allows Dr. Dibya Prabha to see each of the retina's distinctive layers, mapping and measuring their exact thickness. This state-of-the-art machine, available right here at Palamu Neuro & Eye Care, has transformed the early diagnosis of blinding eye diseases.
whyItIsDone: To detect the earliest microscopic signs of macular degeneration (ARMD) before vision is lost
To precisely measure retinal swelling (macular edema) commonly caused by diabetic retinopathy
To accurately diagnose and monitor the progression of glaucoma by analyzing optic nerve fiber thickness
To identify the presence and exact size of a macular hole or epiretinal membrane prior to surgery

procedureSteps.title: Positioning
procedureSteps.description: You sit comfortably in front of the OCT machine. Your chin rests on a support and your forehead against a bar — similar to a slit-lamp exam.

procedureSteps.title: Dilation (sometimes)
procedureSteps.description: For some scans, your pupils may be dilated with eye drops for a wider view of the retina. Many modern OCT machines can scan through undilated pupils as well.

procedureSteps.title: Scanning
procedureSteps.description: You focus on a target light (a dot or crosshair) while the OCT machine scans your retina. The scan takes only seconds per eye. You may see a faint red line moving across your vision — this is the scanning beam.

procedureSteps.title: Analysis & Review
procedureSteps.description: Dr. Dibya Prabha immediately reviews the high-resolution cross-sectional and 3D images, explains the findings, and determines if any treatment or monitoring is needed.

preparation: No special preparation is needed for most OCT scans
If dilation is required, bring sunglasses for after the appointment (you'll be sensitive to light for a few hours)
If dilation is used, arrange transportation — your vision will be blurry for 2–4 hours
Bring your current glasses or contact lens prescription if available
Inform the doctor of any medications you are taking, especially hydroxychloroquine

faqs.question: What is OCTA and how is it different from OCT?
faqs.answer: OCTA (OCT Angiography) is an advanced form of OCT that specifically visualizes blood flow in the retina and choroid — without any dye injection. While standard OCT shows retinal structure (layers), OCTA shows retinal blood vessels and can detect abnormal blood vessel growth, blocked vessels, and areas of poor circulation. It provides information similar to traditional fluorescein angiography but is faster, dye-free, and completely non-invasive.

faqs.question: Who needs an OCTA scan?
faqs.answer: OCTA is particularly valuable for patients with diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration (to detect abnormal blood vessels), retinal vein occlusions, and other retinal vascular diseases. It helps Dr. Dibya Prabha detect disease earlier and monitor treatment response more precisely.

faqs.question: Is OCTA scan safe?
faqs.answer: Yes, OCTA is very safe. Unlike traditional fluorescein angiography, OCTA does not require dye injection, so there is no risk of allergic reaction, no nausea, and no needle. It uses the same safe light-based technology as standard OCT.

whatIsIt: Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA) is an advanced imaging technology that provides a highly detailed, 3D view of the blood vessel networks within the retina—without the need to inject any fluorescent dye into your arm. By analyzing the motion of red blood cells, this cutting-edge scanner at our Palamu clinic allows Dr. Dibya Prabha to instantly detect abnormal vascular growth or blocked vessels in the eye.
whyItIsDone: To safely and painlessly detect the abnormal, leaking blood vessels characteristic of Wet Macular Degeneration
To evaluate the microscopic areas of oxygen deprivation (ischemia) in advanced Diabetic Retinopathy
To accurately diagnose vascular occlusions (eye strokes) where blood flow to the retina is suddenly blocked
To closely monitor the effectiveness of anti-VEGF eye injections over time

procedureSteps.title: Positioning
procedureSteps.description: You sit comfortably at the OCTA machine with your chin on the chin rest and forehead against the support bar.

procedureSteps.title: Fixation
procedureSteps.description: You focus on a target light while the machine performs rapid, repeated OCT scans. No dye, no injection, no contact with the eye.

procedureSteps.title: Acquisition
procedureSteps.description: The machine captures thousands of scans over a small area of your retina in just a few seconds. Motion correction software ensures clear images even if you blink or move slightly.

procedureSteps.title: Review
procedureSteps.description: Dr. Dibya Prabha reviews the 3D vascular maps, identifies areas of abnormal blood flow or vessel growth, and discusses findings and treatment decisions immediately.

preparation: No special preparation is needed — no fasting, no dye, no IV
If dilation is required, bring sunglasses for after your appointment
Bring a list of current medications, especially blood thinners or diabetes medications
The test takes only 5–10 minutes for both eyes

faqs.question: What is fundus photography?
faqs.answer: Fundus photography is a specialized medical imaging technique that captures detailed, high-resolution color photographs of the retina (the back of the eye), including the optic nerve, macula, and retinal blood vessels. It creates a permanent visual record for disease monitoring and comparison over time.

faqs.question: Why is fundus photography done?
faqs.answer: Fundus photography documents the current state of the retina for comparison at future visits — essential for monitoring progressive conditions like diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and macular degeneration. It also helps educate patients by showing them what their retina looks like and explaining visible changes.

faqs.question: How long does fundus photography take?
faqs.answer: The actual photography takes only a few minutes. Including dilation (if needed) and the overall eye examination, plan for 20–30 minutes at Palamu Neuro & Eye Care.

whatIsIt: Fundus Photography involves capturing high-resolution, color images of the interior surface of the eye, known as the fundus. This includes the retina, macula, optic disc, and the delicate blood vessels supplying them. At Palamu Neuro & Eye Care, Dr. Dibya Prabha uses these detailed photographs to establish a visual baseline of your eye health, allowing her to carefully monitor the microscopic progression of diseases over months or years.
whyItIsDone: To document the exact severity and stage of diabetic retinopathy for future comparison
To track the slow growth or changes in a choroidal nevus (an eye freckle) to ensure it is not becoming cancerous
To monitor the structural changes in the optic nerve that occur progressively in glaucoma
To educate patients by visually showing them the exact condition of their own retina

procedureSteps.title: Pupil Dilation
procedureSteps.description: Eye drops are instilled to dilate your pupils for a wide, clear view of the retina. Dilation takes 15–20 minutes to fully take effect.

procedureSteps.title: Positioning
procedureSteps.description: You sit at the fundus camera with your chin on the chin rest and forehead against the support bar — very similar to a slit-lamp exam.

procedureSteps.title: Image Capture
procedureSteps.description: You look at a fixation target while the camera captures images. A brief flash of light indicates each photo being taken. Multiple images are captured of different retinal areas. The process takes 2–5 minutes.

procedureSteps.title: Review
procedureSteps.description: Dr. Dibya Prabha reviews the images immediately, compares them to any previous photographs, and discusses the findings with you.

preparation: Bring sunglasses — your eyes will be light-sensitive for 2–4 hours after dilation
Arrange transportation if possible — dilated pupils make driving difficult and potentially unsafe
Bring your previous eye records or fundus photographs if taken elsewhere
No fasting or other special preparation is required
